messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] Diagonal covariance structure and crossed random effects
messages.subject_clean: Diagonal covariance structure and crossed random effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

In lme4 2.0-1, the diag tag only suppresses estimation of the correlation in
m1, but not in m2:

item <- factor(rep(1:10, each = 18))
m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + diag(Days | Subject) + (1 | item), sleepstudy)
m2 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | item) + diag(Days | Subject), sleepstudy)

logLik(m1)  # 'log Lik.' -871.756 (df=6)
logLik(m2)  # 'log Lik.' -871.7482 (df=7)

Seemingly, depending on the order of the two random-effect terms one
gets different models. Is this intended behavior?

Best, Florian

(I apologize if this is known and fixed already. Maybe it's related to
https://github.com/lme4/lme4/issues/945. Also, sorry for not posting on
GitHub, I do not have an account.)

messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in R – Online course, 21–24 September
messages.subject_clean: Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in R – Online course, 21–24 September
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
We are pleased to announce our upcoming online course ?Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in R?, taking place from 21?24 September.
 
Course website: [ https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/glmms-in-r/ ]( https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/glmms-in-r/ ) 
 
Instructor: [ Prof. Florian Hartig (University of Regensburg, Germany) ]( https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=AdcDit0AAAAJ )
 
This four-day practical course will provide participants with the knowledge and tools needed to design, interpret, validate, and communicate robust statistical analyses using GLMMs in R.
Throughout the course, participants will learn how to:
Extend linear and generalized linear models by incorporating random effects
Model complex data structures using variance and correlation structures
Select appropriate model formulations for experimental and observational studies
Interpret fitted models and estimate predictor effects
Visualize model predictions and assess model assumptions
The course will cover key concepts including regression modelling, scaling and centering, interactions, contrasts, model selection, generalized linear mixed models, model diagnostics, and approaches for handling spatial, temporal, and phylogenetic autocorrelation.
 
Best regards,
Carlo

messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] Determining prediction (or tolerance) intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Long version below.

For a concrete application, I would like to generate tolerance and
prediction regions of straight lines obtained by mixed-effects linear
regression, with random slope and intercept, and including this
randoms variations also.

Is there any package that allows to do this, like a

md <- lm( Y ~ X, data = d )
predict( md, newdata = dp, interval = "pred" )

for a classical linear model?

** Long version **

The context is to determine limits of blank (LOB), detection (LOD) and
quantification (LOQ) of an analytical method that uses a calibration
curve, Y = a X + b where X is the concentration and Y the observed
value. First step is to find a and b from known (X, Y) values, and
then to determine unknown values X* of X using observed Y values,
hence X* = (Y - b)/a. Of course, X* != X even for training values.

The method is used with different reagents, leading to a
(potential) fixed effect on a and b, and in different centers, leading
to a (potential) random effect on a and b also. Limits (LOB, LOD, LOQ)
should be defined for each reagent, but for an average center, taking
into account between-center variability.

Fitting the model with lmer works quite well, and Gaussian assumptions
are reasonnably met.

LOB is the 0,95 quantile of the X* distribution when X equals 0, which
is one condition available of the data --- so it is the upper limit of
a 95% prediction, or eventually tolerance, unilateral interval.
Currently, I reconstruct it ? by hand ? adapting the basic formula:

IP = m + t * s * sqrt( 1 + 1/n )

with m = average, s = standard deviation, t quantile of a Student
distribution with n-1 ddl and n the sample size. Adaptation is to
define s? as the sum of residual variance and between-center variance,
and usethe Kendall-Rogers approximation of the dl.

Is there anything better than that?

LOD is defined as the lowest X for which the 0.05 quantile of X*
distribution equals the LOB. Hence, it may be obtained by finding the
intersection of the vertical line ? X = LOB ? and the boundary of the
90% prediction interval of the straight line [upper if a > 0, lower if
a < 0].  Hence my question on how to obtain the prediction region of
the straight line, for a given reagent but taking into account both
between-center and residual variability?

Eventually, would ? forgetting ? the random effect and using a
classical linear model, for which predict() works, give a reasonnable
value, or problems of correlations between values would make this
highly unreliable?

Thanks in advance for any help,


 


-- 
                                Emmanuel CURIS
                                emmanuel.curis at parisdescartes.fr

Page WWW: http://emmanuel.curis.online.fr/index.html

Dear all,
 
Join our live online course Markov and Hidden Markov Models with Applications in R, taking place 1?4 September, and learn how to apply one of the most powerful modeling frameworks for longitudinal data.
 
 
Course website: [ https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/markov-and-hidden-markov-models-with-applications-in-r/ ]( https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/markov-and-hidden-markov-models-with-applications-in-r/ ) 
 
 
Over four interactive sessions, you'll combine theory with hands-on practice using the LMest R package. You'll learn how to build, estimate, interpret, and select Markov and Hidden Markov Models for continuous, categorical, and incomplete longitudinal data.
 
Participants will:
Learn the fundamentals of Markov and Hidden Markov Models
Gain practical experience with R and the LMest package
Work through real data examples and interactive exercises
Discover best practices for model selection, interpretation, and reporting
 
Whether you're a researcher, graduate student, or data analyst working in academia, industry, or consultancy, this course will provide practical skills you can immediately apply to your own data.
 
 
Best regards,
 
Carlo
